definition: Contradict means to assert the opposite of a statement, or to be inconsistent with it.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word contradict. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know contradict should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: New sailors quickly learn that it is risky to contradict the captain on deck.
To question a statement is only to ask whether it is true; to contradict it is to assert the opposite outright.
To contradict a claim is to declare it wrong; to refute it is to prove it wrong.

Gainsay is the formal, slightly antique word for denying or disputing, and it lives almost entirely in negative constructions: no one could gainsay her record. Contradict is the everyday working word, and the blunter act — you contradict someone by stating the opposite to their face.

Negate means to deny something or cancel it out — one fact can negate another, and a late penalty negates a lead. It works on validity, often silently and on paper. Contradict works out loud: to contradict a claim is to assert the opposite of it, usually in front of the person who made it.

Rebut means to argue against a claim with evidence — lawyers and debaters rebut, bringing proof and structured argument. Contradict needs no evidence at all: you contradict a statement simply by asserting the opposite. A rebuttal is built; a contradiction is just declared.

Contradict means to assert the opposite of a statement, or to be inconsistent with it.
The intern chose not to contradict the senior engineer, even though the blueprints clearly showed a different measurement.
To contradict the engineer would be to state, out loud, the opposite of what he said.
The infinitive 'to contradict' shows the act being weighed as a choice — one the intern decides against.

Contradict takes a direct object — you contradict someone or something — unlike disagree, which needs 'with.' Contradicting a person to their face is blunter and more confrontational than merely disagreeing with them, which is why so many sentences pair it with hesitation: 'didn't dare to contradict,' 'was reluctant to contradict.'

For her history project, Amara set out to tell the story of the old mill at the edge of town.
The official plaque by the river was confident: the mill burned down in 1902 and was never rebuilt.
But the boxes in the library basement told another story.
A 1911 photograph showed the mill standing, its wheel turning and workers lined up at the door.
A ledger from 1915 listed wages paid to mill hands, and a yellowed newspaper from the same year advertised the mill's flour at the fall fair.
Every new source seemed to contradict the plaque, and Amara realized her project had changed: she was no longer retelling the town's story but correcting it.
